hypotheses.statement: Coralito Flats has a genuine physical-layer defect in its serial/daisy-chain comms network (marginal terminations, connector corrosion, or grounding/surge exposure) concentrated in a few blocks, producing repeat self-clearing dropouts on the same assets and zones.

Other symptoms on the same assets (tracker misalignment, inverter derate) should be rare or absent, i.e. the assets themselves are healthy while only the comms path fails.
Comms-module and surge-card parts consumption at this site should exceed the fleet per-GW-month rate.
discriminating_evidence: Asset-level repeat count: high concentration (few assets, many hits) supports H1; 13 distinct assets spread across the site undercuts it.
Presence of hardware parts issued or physical repairs (reseat, replace) versus pure RESET/NO-FAULT-FOUND closures.
Whether comms_loss WOs at this site trend upward over time (degrading physical layer) or stay flat.

Narratives should repeatedly assert the asset was operating normally while showing offline ('inverting fine', 'come back on their own', 'no production lost').
Priority distribution should skew P3/P4, inconsistent with a fault causing real generation loss.
discriminating_evidence: Any member WO with material reported lost_mwh or a confirmed production stoppage would falsify H2 and favour H1.
Compare lost_mwh per comms_loss WO at Coralito versus fleet comms_loss WOs: if Coralito's is materially lower, the site is logging events other sites ignore.
Presence versus absence of parts issued: sustained zero-parts closures support H2.

Tech mobility check — comms_loss rate follows the technician between sites (H3) or stays with the site regardless of technician (H1/H2).
Count of members that are group/blanket logs versus single-asset incidents.

Site-level cooling-system PM history: if the affected skids had overdue or skipped HVAC/filter PMs, this becomes a maintenance-driven variant rather than pure weather

hypotheses.statement: Sundowner Mesa's tracker rows have a real structural or stow-control weakness (dampers, purlins, limit-switch brackets, stow pins) that fails at wind speeds other fleet sites survive, and the March event merely exposed a pre-existing defect population.
predictions: A recurring, narrow component vocabulary dominates the narratives ('bent damper', 'bent purlin north end', 'limit switch bracket bent') at far higher share than tracker_mechanical_damage narratives elsewhere in the fleet.
Repeat work orders appear against the same asset_id or same block after an initial repair (WO-2025-00286 already carries recurrence=true), including on dates with no storm mention.
Some tracker_mechanical_damage work orders at this site predate 2025-03-14 or postdate the event backlog with environment='none_mentioned' and no event reference.
Resolution codes skew toward ADJUSTED/RESET/straighten-and-retorque rather than engineered replacement, implying repeated re-failure of the same members.
If the fleet contains other sites with the same tracker vendor/model, those sites show elevated (though possibly lower) tracker_mechanical_damage rates too.
discriminating_evidence: Rate of new damage on the same repaired assets in the 90 days after repair: non-trivial recurrence supports H2, near-zero recurrence supports H1.
Existence of any tracker_mechanical_damage work orders at Sundowner Mesa in a clean pre-event window.
Comparison of same-storm damage counts per GW at neighbouring sites: Sundowner Mesa materially worse than peers under equal exposure points to H2.

hypotheses.statement: The count of 20 is inflated by work-order bookkeeping rather than by 20 distinct failures: duplicate/re-logged tickets and mixed asset granularity (zone-level TR-Zxx tickets covering nine rows each alongside single-row TR-Bxx-Rxxx tickets) make the per-GW-month rate non-comparable to the fleet baseline.
predictions: At least two members carry near-identical narrative text against the same asset (WO-2025-00278 and WO-2025-00293 both read 'TR-Z02 ... Nine rows needed attention, mostly clamps and dampers ... except two rows'), and similar pairing exists for TR-Z09 (WO-2025-00258, WO-2025-00387).
The asset_id field mixes two granularities within one cluster: zone identifiers (TR-Z02, TR-Z09) and row identifiers (TR-B01-R039), which does not occur in the fleet comparison population.

Total labor 80.9 h across 20 work orders (~4 h each) is low for 20 independent structural repairs, and the zone-level tickets carry the largest hour counts (8.9, 7.1, 6.2, 5.1), consistent with a few campaigns split across many tickets.

Exposure of only 5.3 GW-months implies a short observation window or recent onboarding; the site's total work-order history should be correspondingly thin, making any per-GW-month rate statistically unstable.
Deduplicating on (asset_id, narrative fingerprint) and normalising zone tickets to one event each should cut effective n materially, reducing lift well below 23x.
discriminating_evidence: Manual dedup pass: if collapsing duplicate and zone-level tickets drops n from 20 to roughly 10-14, the lift is partly artifactual; if all 20 map to distinct assets and distinct repair actions, H3 is weak.
Check whether other fleet sites log zone-level tracker tickets at all; if only Sundowner Mesa does, the denominator/numerator mismatch is confirmed.
Poisson interval on n=20 over 5.3 GW-months versus the fleet rate: if the lower bound still exceeds the fleet rate by an order of magnitude even after dedup, H3 cannot explain the whole signal.

hypotheses.statement: An open insurance property claim (ref NRS-PL-2025-0417) drove one-work-order-per-row documentation at this site, so the cluster reflects a claim-documentation reporting practice, not a higher physical damage rate than comparable events elsewhere in the fleet.
predictions: A claim reference number appears in the narratives of members at this site and appears in few or no tracker work orders at other sites.

Work orders in this cluster are disproportionately authored by a small number of technicians (TECH-0231 dominates the sample), indicating a single documentation convention rather than site-wide practice.
Members include tickets with action='inspected_only' or outcome='pending' and no parts consumed, i.e. documentation/photo visits logged as corrective work orders (WO-2025-00214, WO-2025-00258).
Reported lost MWh (28.0 total, ~1.4 per work order) is small relative to 20 supposed structural failures, consistent with many tickets covering the same physical downtime.

Parts consumption is sparse and often inconsistent with the narrative (e.g. 'tracker motor x3' logged against a photo-and-measure ticket; 'damper' logged against a bracket reform), suggesting parts were booked to claim lines rather than to the described repair.
discriminating_evidence: Compare work-orders-per-affected-row at Sundowner Mesa post-event with the same ratio at any other site that had a documented storm claim; a higher ratio here isolates a reporting effect.
Restrict the cluster to tickets with action='repaired_in_place' or 'part_replaced' and non-empty parts_used, then recompute the rate; a large drop supports H4.
If the elevated ticket rate ends abruptly on the claim closure date rather than decaying with physical repair progress, H4 is favoured over H1.

hypotheses.statement: A genuine structural defect exists in a subset of Sundowner Mesa rows — torque-tube/bearing misalignment at or near the third bearing in blocks B02 and B05 — driven by a common foundation-settlement or bearing/damper batch issue, and it is distinct from the generic controller recalibrations in the same cluster.
predictions: The structural subset (component=tracker_structure, parts: damper/bearing housing/coupling) should be spatially concentrated: asset_ids clustered in B02/B05 and in adjacent row numbers (e.g. R057/R058), not uniformly spread across B01–B08.

Repeat or follow-on work orders should appear on the same or neighbouring rows within 6–12 months, even if the 'recurrence' flag is currently false (check asset_id reappearance across all symptoms, not just tracker_misalignment).
Structural cases should carry systematically higher labor_hours and parts consumption than controller cases (3.8 vs 1.7 h is the wrong direction here — needs to hold across the full population).
Other symptoms on the same assets (e.g. tracker_stall, abnormal_noise, motor_overcurrent) should be elevated at Sundowner Mesa relative to fleet, since a bent torque tube loads the drive train.
If foundation-related, commissioning-era or PM work orders on those rows should mention pier, grout, or level checks.
discriminating_evidence: Asset-level geographic clustering: if the 7 WOs map to a contiguous block/row band, defect is favoured; if scattered evenly across blocks, artifact/noise is favoured.
Recurrence on the same asset_id after 'resolved' closure — a real structural defect should not stay fixed by shimming.
Presence of the same 'third bearing' language on assets handled by techs other than TECH-0231; if the phrase only ever appears from one tech, it is a phrasing artifact rather than a physical finding.

hypotheses.statement: The cluster is largely a reporting/logging artifact: one technician (TECH-0231, 5 of 7 WOs) uses copy-pasted narrative templates and a loose 'tracker_misalignment' label, inflating Sundowner Mesa's count for a symptom other sites log under different symptom codes or as routine PM.
predictions: Verbatim-identical narrative strings should recur across distinct asset_ids (already visible: three WOs share 'torque tube out of true at the third bearing. Shimmed and realigned.' on TR-B05-R024, TR-B02-R072, TR-B02-R057).
Removing TECH-0231's work orders should drop Sundowner Mesa's tracker_misalignment rate to near or below the fleet rate of 0.39/GW-month.
TECH-0231 should show above-average use of the tracker_misalignment code across every site they have worked, not just Sundowner Mesa.
Other sites should show a compensating excess in adjacent symptom codes (tracker_stall, tracker_no_response, controller_fault) such that the combined tracker-symptom rate is comparable fleet-wide.

Field inconsistency should be widespread in this tech's records: resolution_code=PART-REPL with empty parts_used (WO-2025-01179, WO-2026-00073 pattern), or RESET/ADJUSTED codes paired with hardware parts.
discriminating_evidence: Tech-stratified rate: compute tracker_misalignment per GW-month with and without TECH-0231; a large collapse implicates the reporter, stability implicates the site.
Cross-site behaviour of TECH-0231 and TECH-0194 — if they carry the elevated rate with them to other sites, the site is not the cause.
Fleet-wide count of exact duplicate narrative strings: if templating is uniform across the fleet, it explains labelling but not the 3.4x lift; if concentrated at this site/tech, it explains both.

hypotheses.statement: This is ordinary Poisson variation on a small denominator: 7 events against an expected ~2.1 over only 5.3 GW-months is within the range a fleet-wide multiple-comparisons scan will throw up by chance, possibly compounded by understated exposure for this site.
predictions: The 95% interval on 7 counts is roughly 2.8–14 events, i.e. a rate band of ~0.53–2.7/GW-month, which overlaps or sits close to several other sites' observed rates — other site|symptom candidates in the same scan should show similar lifts at similar n.
The 7 events should be roughly uniform in time (observed: Mar, Apr x2, Aug, Sep, Dec, Jan) with no burst structure — consistent with a homogeneous Poisson process, not a triggered failure wave.
Sundowner Mesa should NOT be elevated across other symptom families; the excess should be confined to this one cell.
If exposure_gw_months is recomputed from actual commissioned capacity and in-service dates, the rate should move materially toward 0.39.
discriminating_evidence: Re-run the scan on a held-out time window (e.g. only 2026 data, or only H1 2025): a chance cluster will not reproduce its lift, a real one will.
Count how many site|symptom cells were tested; if hundreds, a lift of 3.4 at n=7 is expected to occur several times by chance.
Audit the exposure denominator — partial-year energisation or block-level derating would explain the lift with no failure-side cause at all.

hypotheses.statement: Sundowner Mesa is a high-wind, exposed-mesa site, and the misalignment work orders are expected wind-loading wear on dampers, bearings and couplings rather than a defect — normal maintenance whose rate is simply higher at windier sites.
predictions: Wind-related parts (damper, bearing housing, coupling) should dominate parts_used at this site across all symptoms, not just tracker_misalignment.
Event dates should cluster around seasonal high-wind or stow-event periods (spring in the desert Southwest: note Mar/Apr x2 here) with a quieter summer, and stow-related WOs should co-occur.
Other exposed sites in the fleet should show a similar tracker_misalignment lift, so the fleet rate should be bimodal by site exposure rather than Sundowner Mesa being a lone outlier.
Narratives at this site should mention wind, stow, gust, or dust in the environment field at above-fleet frequency — currently ALL seven are 'none_mentioned', which counts against this hypothesis.
discriminating_evidence: The environment extraction field: seven of seven 'none_mentioned' is direct evidence against a weather driver, unless extraction is known to under-capture environment mentions — test extraction recall on a labelled sample.
Temporal correlation between misalignment WOs and site stow/high-wind alarm events in the same work-order stream.
Compare Sundowner Mesa's rate against other sites sharing the same tracker OEM and terrain class; if only this site is elevated, environment is not sufficient.

hypotheses.statement: There is no KVP-3600-specific ground-fault problem: 33 events across 376 units (0.088/unit vs peer median 0.080, lift 1.1) is ordinary variation in a generic, high-frequency symptom that every inverter model in the fleet reports at a similar rate.
predictions: Ranking all model|symptom pairs, ground_fault appears in the top few symptoms for most models, not just KVP-3600.
A binomial/Poisson interval on 33/376 overlaps the peer median rate (0.08); the excess is ~3 work orders over 2.5+ years.
Per-unit ground-fault counts are near-Poisson: mostly 0, a few 1, essentially no units with 3+ repeats (recurrence=false throughout).
Mean labor_hours (5.1) and lost MWh per event for KVP-3600 ground faults are within the fleet distribution for the same symptom on other models.
Events are spread thinly across many sites (12+ sites in a 14-record sample) with no site contributing a disproportionate share after normalising by units installed.
discriminating_evidence: Compute rate per unit-year rather than per unit; if KVP-3600 fleet age or commissioning date is similar to peers and the rate still sits at ~1.1x, the signal dies.
If instead a specific serial block or site shows 3-5x the fleet rate, H1 is falsified in favour of H2.
If ground_fault rate for KVP-3600 exceeds peers only in one calendar quarter, H1 loses to H4/environmental.

hypotheses.statement: A real but installation-side defect exists: DC home runs and string connectors at combiner boxes are being chafed or pinched (rack uprights, gland entries), producing genuine earth faults concentrated in specific combiner positions, sites, or install vintages rather than in the KVP-3600 inverter itself.
predictions: Roughly half or more of the 33 narratives name a physical cause at a combiner (CB-Bxx-yy) — chafed home run or pinched connector — and close with repaired_in_place or part_replaced.
The named combiner IDs cluster in a limited set of positions/rows rather than being uniform across all CB numbers at a site.
The same physical-cause narratives should appear on non-KVP models at sites built by the same EPC/installer, i.e. the pattern tracks site/vintage, not model.
Asset-ID vintage digits (e.g. 16xx/17xx vs 24xx) should show a skew: one build era carries a disproportionate share of chafe/pinch findings.
Physical-cause events should have higher labor_hours and higher lost_mwh than the reset-only events in the same cluster.
discriminating_evidence: Cross-tab cause-type (physical vs no-fault-found) against site and installer/vintage: if physical causes concentrate in a few sites shared with other inverter models, the defect is racking/harness, not KVP-3600.
If chafe/pinch findings are evenly distributed across all sites and vintages at background rate, H2 collapses back to H1.
Repeat ground faults on the same asset_id or same combiner ID would strongly support an unresolved systemic routing defect.

hypotheses.statement: The cluster is partly a bookkeeping artifact: resolution_code, narrative text, and NLP-extracted fields contradict each other (RESET codes on connector replacements, NO-FAULT-FOUND codes on part replacements, 'central_inverter'/'string_inverter' component tags on string-walk jobs), so the 33 records do not represent one coherent failure mode and may include templated or duplicated entries.
predictions: A direct cross-tab of resolution_code against extracted.action shows disagreement in a large fraction of the 33 records (e.g. RESET paired with part_replaced, NO-FAULT-FOUND paired with part_replaced).
Several narratives are near-verbatim copies differing only in asset_id and combiner ID ('tripped on DC GF. Traced it to a pinched connector in CB-...'), indicating template or copy-paste entry.
parts_used is blank on most records that the narrative says had a connector replaced — parts consumption does not corroborate the stated repairs.
extracted.component disagrees with the component named in the narrative in a measurable share of records (inverter tagged where only strings/combiners were touched).
The same code/narrative disagreement rate appears for other models' ground-fault records, showing it is a corpus-wide coding hygiene issue, not KVP-specific.
discriminating_evidence: Split the 33 into (a) narrative-confirmed physical fault and (b) reset-only/no-fault-found; if the split is roughly even, the 'cluster' is two populations and its rate should be recomputed per sub-population before any lift claim.
If parts inventory issuance records match the claimed connector replacements, the narratives are trustworthy and H3 weakens.
If duplicate-text detection finds identical narratives on distinct assets and dates, at least part of the count is template noise.

hypotheses.statement: The no-fault-found subset (walked strings, meggered OK, reset held) is nuisance tripping from transient insulation leakage — morning dew, humidity, or high-ambient-heat conditions pushing leakage past the detector threshold — not a hardware defect, and it inflates the ground_fault count without any physical failure.
predictions: A substantial subset of the 33 records carry resolution_code NO-FAULT-FOUND or RESET with action reset_or_restart, outcome resolved, recurrence false, and blank parts_used.
These reset-only events cluster by date/season or by narrow date windows shared across multiple sites (several assets tripping within the same few days).
Reset-only events have low lost_mwh and shorter downtime than physical-cause events, since restoration is immediate after reset.
environment tags of high_ambient_heat or moisture-related terms should appear more often in reset-only records than in chafe/pinch records if the trigger is climatic.
Peer inverter models at the same sites should show a matching burst of reset-only ground faults on the same dates.
discriminating_evidence: Plot event dates for reset-only vs physical-cause subsets: temporal clustering in the former plus a flat distribution in the latter separates H4 from H2.
If reset-only ground faults on the same dates also hit non-KVP models at the same sites, the driver is environmental/site-wide, not model-specific.
If reset-only events are uniformly distributed year-round and show no cross-site coincidence, H4 fails and the resets are better explained by H3 (mis-coding) or H1.

hypotheses.statement: The 51% fleet baseline is not a comparable denominator: TECH-0231's queue is almost purely tracker work (where a row asset ID exists), while the fleet figure pools work types/assets for which row-level tagging is impossible or meaningless, so the 91% vs 51% gap is a work-mix artifact rather than a behavioural difference.
predictions: Restricting the fleet baseline to tracker-component work orders only (component in tracker_structure/tracker_drive/tracker_motor/tracker_controller) should move fleet row-share from 0.51 toward 0.85-0.95, collapsing the gap.
TECH-0231's own work orders should show near-zero non-tracker components; the 41 members should be almost entirely tracker components (as in the sample, 14/14).
Other technicians whose WOs are filtered to tracker-only work should also show row-share well above 0.51.
Non-tracker WOs fleet-wide should show asset IDs at inverter/combiner/block granularity, not TR-Bxx-Rxxx.
discriminating_evidence: Compute row-share per technician within tracker-only work orders: if TECH-0231 is unremarkable there, H1 explains the flag and H2/H3/H4 are not needed.
If TECH-0231 still sits far above peers after work-type stratification, H1 is falsified.

hypotheses.statement: The 'granularity' field is derived from narrative text parsing, and TECH-0231 simply has the habit of opening every narrative with the row tag ("TR-B0x-Rxxx ..."), so the metric measures writing style rather than actual CMMS asset assignment.
predictions: In TECH-0231's records the asset_id field should be reproducible from the first token of the narrative in a very high fraction of rows (13/14 in the sample begin with the row tag).
Technicians with low row-share should show narratives that mention rows in free text but carry block- or site-level asset_id values, i.e. narrative and asset_id disagree more often.
Other TECH-0231 metadata should show similar template regularity (repeated stock phrases such as 'verified through a full sweep', which appears in ~6/14 sampled narratives).

Extraction noise should be visible independently: sampled rows already contain resolution_code/action contradictions (NO-FAULT-FOUND with 'part_replaced', 'tracker motor x3' as parts on a damper job), indicating the structured fields are partly machine-inferred.
discriminating_evidence: Check whether asset_id was entered at WO creation (dispatch timestamp) or populated later/derived; if asset_id predates the narrative, style cannot be the cause and H2 fails.
Compare field-level provenance: if low-row-share techs' narratives contain row tags at the same rate as TECH-0231's, the difference is parsing/entry, not observation.

hypotheses.statement: A discrete high-wind event on 2025-03-14 at Sundowner Mesa generated an insurance claim (NRS-PL-2025-0417) that required per-row damage documentation, and TECH-0231 was the assigned claim technician, so the row-level logging is a time-bounded claim-handling artifact concentrated in the Mar-Jun 2025 window.
predictions: TECH-0231's row-share should be strongly time-varying: near 1.0 for WOs dated 2025-03-15 through roughly 2025-06, and closer to the fleet baseline for 2026 WOs.
A disproportionate share of the 41 members should cluster at Sundowner Mesa in a ~10-week block after 2025-03-14, with tracker_mechanical_damage symptoms.
Other technicians working the same event window at Sundowner Mesa should also show elevated row-share, and their row-share should drop afterward too.
Claim references or 'event/cleanup' language should co-occur with the earliest members (present in WO-2025-00214 and WO-2025-00368).
discriminating_evidence: Split TECH-0231's 41 WOs into pre/post 2025-07 cohorts: if 2026 WOs (e.g. Ashvale Dry Lake, Joshua Fork) still run ~90% row-level, the event cannot be the driver and H3 loses to H1/H2/H4.
Check whether row-share elevation is shared with other techs in the same event window (event-driven) or unique to TECH-0231 (personal habit).

hypotheses.statement: The effect is a site/assignment confound: the three sites TECH-0231 works (Sundowner Mesa, Joshua Fork, Ashvale Dry Lake) have their tracker assets registered down to the row in the CMMS hierarchy, while other fleet sites are registered at block level, so any technician assigned there would show ~90% row-level logging.
predictions: Row-share computed per site should be near 0.9 at Sundowner Mesa, Joshua Fork and Ashvale Dry Lake and well below 0.51 at the remaining fleet sites.
Other technicians with WOs at these three sites should show row-share statistically indistinguishable from TECH-0231's 0.91.
The asset register for these sites should contain distinct TR-Bxx-Rxxx entries; low-row-share sites should have no such per-row asset records to select.
If TECH-0231 has any WOs at a block-level site, those specific WOs should be logged at block granularity.
discriminating_evidence: Fit row-share by site and by technician jointly: if the site term absorbs the effect and the technician term shrinks to noise, H4 wins over H2.
Look for a technician at these sites with low row-share; a single such counterexample argues the registry permits both granularities and pushes the explanation back to individual habit (H2).

hypotheses.statement: KVP-3600 inverters carry a cooling/fan-control or thermal-threshold defect (likely firmware-set derate point, not blocked airflow) that causes an unlogged 10-12% afternoon power limit at high ambient, and it is progressive/recurring on the same units regardless of fan or filter replacement.
predictions: Repeat WOs on the same asset IDs across separate seasons (e.g. KVP36-2419B-0361 appears in 2024-09 and 2025-07); recurrence flag true on a majority of members.

Members where parts were actually consumed ('cooling fan x3', 'air filter set') generate a follow-up thermal_derate WO on the same asset within the next hot season, i.e. no measurable benefit_pct anywhere in the cluster.
Resolution codes stay in the ESCALATED / VENDOR-REFERRED / NO-FAULT-FOUND family with outcome 'pending' or 'no_change'; essentially zero 'REPAIRED' closures.
Affected units share a serial/build band or firmware revision field; unaffected KVP-3600s in the same cohort at equally hot sites cluster in a different band.
Cluster count grows year-over-year (1 in 2024, 3 in 2025, 3 in 2026 by June) faster than cohort growth.
discriminating_evidence: A firmware/serial field that splits the 7 affected units from the ~369 unaffected ones at comparable site temperature separates H1 from H3/H4.
If any unit was fully repaired (fan controller or board swap) and then produced no further thermal_derate WO in the following summer, H1 is supported and H3 (as-designed behaviour) is weakened.
If peer-model inverters at the SAME sites also log afternoon derate WOs on the same dates, H1 loses to H4.

hypotheses.statement: The cluster is largely a text/extraction artifact: several narratives are verbatim or near-verbatim copies of one another and three of seven come from a single technician, so 'thermal_derate' is a labelling convention applied to KVP units rather than a distinct physical event population.
predictions: String-similarity check finds byte-identical or >95% identical narrative bodies across WO-2024-00163 / WO-2025-00720 and across WO-2025-00688 / WO-2025-00908 / WO-2026-00571 / WO-2026-00586.
Author concentration: TECH-0103 authors 3/7 members; the whole cluster is written by <=6 distinct techs out of the site technician population.

Peer models show non-zero counts of a semantically equivalent symptom under a different key (e.g. 'low_output', 'underperformance', 'high_temp'), so the peer_median_rate of 0.0 is a taxonomy artifact rather than a real absence.
Component field is internally inconsistent (one member tagged 'string_inverter', the rest 'central_inverter') for the same model, indicating field-fill noise.
Environment tags split between 'high_ambient_heat' and 'none_mentioned' on narratives describing the same afternoon-heat scenario.
discriminating_evidence: Run exact-duplicate detection on narrative text: if the templated WOs are removed, does n drop below ~4 and the rate become indistinguishable from peers?
Re-map peer-model symptom keys onto a common vocabulary; if peer rate rises to ~0.015-0.02, the lift disappears and H2 explains the candidate without any defect.
Rate of thermal_derate per technician-authored WO: if it is flat across techs, H2 weakens; if it is driven by one or two authors, H2 is favoured.

hypotheses.statement: This is the inverter's designed high-ambient protection operating normally — cabinet temperature rises through the afternoon and recovers after sundown with no stored fault — and the WOs reflect operator unfamiliarity rather than a failure.
predictions: Derate magnitude is tightly clustered (10-12% reported in every narrative) rather than dispersed or worsening, consistent with a fixed spec curve.
Every event self-resolves after sundown with no intervention; no member shows a hard trip, no fault code stored, no parts required to restore output.
Total lost energy is small and bounded: 20.4 MWh over 7 events (~2.9 MWh each), of the order of a few afternoon hours of partial curtailment, not an outage.
All members fall in the hot half of the year (June-September) with none in October-May.
Inspection-only actions ('all six fans turning, filters and plenum clear') find no physical fault in the units that were thoroughly checked.
discriminating_evidence: Compare cabinet-temperature-vs-output on an affected unit against a healthy same-model unit at the same site and hour: if both derate identically, H3 holds and H1 falls.
Check DC:AC ratio / nameplate loading at the affected positions — if derating units are systematically the most heavily loaded, H3 is supported.
If any unit derates at ambient temperatures well below the published operating envelope, H3 is falsified in favour of H1.

hypotheses.statement: Ordinary variation plus discrete summer heat events: 7 events in 376 units (1.9% over ~2 years) is an unremarkable rate, and the apparent model specificity comes from KVP-3600 being concentrated at the hottest sites (Bitter Draw, Ashvale Dry Lake, Joshua Fork) rather than from any model property.
predictions: Member dates concentrate on a small number of calendar days/weeks that coincide with site-wide heat-related WO spikes across all asset classes (tracker, transformer, comms).
Site mix of the KVP-3600 cohort is skewed toward desert/high-ambient sites relative to peer-model cohorts; peer models with zero thermal_derate WOs are installed predominantly at cooler sites.
After stratifying by site (or by site-season), the KVP-3600 thermal_derate rate falls within the range of same-site peer models.
No single asset dominates: excluding the one repeat asset, the remaining events are one-per-unit and spread across 4 sites.
Poisson expectation for 376 units over the observation window makes 7 events unsurprising; comparable clusters of n=5-8 exist for other model-symptom pairs with equally 'null' lift.
discriminating_evidence: Site-stratified rate comparison: if same-site peer models also show ~2% thermal derate, H4 explains everything and H1 is unnecessary.
If the cluster spans many independent hot days across three summers rather than 2-3 discrete heat waves, the 'discrete weather event' part of H4 weakens.
If KVP-3600 units at cool-climate sites also produce thermal_derate WOs, H4 falls and H1 or H3 is favoured.

hypotheses.statement: The entire 27-ticket burst is the remediation tail of a single discrete convective wind event (microburst) on 2025-03-14, not an emerging failure mode, and ticket arrival decays to baseline within ~8-10 weeks with no further wind-independent tracker_structure tickets.
predictions: Zero tracker_structure CM tickets at Sundowner Mesa with open dates before 2025-03-14 in the preceding 8-12 weeks beyond the site's normal 1-3/month baseline; burst_share of 0.84 should mean the remaining 16% is spread thin across all prior months.

Ticket arrival rate declines monotonically after the first two weeks (peak 3/15-3/23, thinning through late April) rather than holding flat or rising - consistent with a fixed damage population being worked down, not a generative process.
Affected asset_ids are spatially clustered (narratives cite 'west side', 'west two thirds of the zone', blocks B01-B09 and zones Z02/Z08/Z09), not uniformly distributed across all blocks.
A single property-claim reference (NRS-PL-2025-0417) appears on the earliest, highest-labor tickets and the damage-only inspection walkdowns.

Failure modes are heterogeneous mechanical overload signatures (bent dampers, bent purlins, bent torque tubes, pulled-through clamps, bent limit-switch brackets) rather than one repeated part failing.
discriminating_evidence: Whether any tracker_structure mechanical-damage ticket at this site opens after ~June 2025 without a high_wind or storm environment tag - if the tail truly ends, H1 survives and H2 weakens.
Whether the same asset_ids re-appear in later wind events at lower recorded wind speeds (supports H2 over H1).
Whether prior-year records show a comparable burst at this site after any prior wind event (recurring event response = H1; first-ever = ambiguous).

hypotheses.statement: The trackers at Sundowner Mesa have a design or installation weakness - rows failing to reach full stow, plus undersized dampers and limit-switch brackets - so a sub-design-wind event produced damage that a compliant tracker population would not have sustained, and the same modes will recur at lower wind speeds.
predictions: Narratives explicitly recording incomplete stow ('rows caught partway to stow') appear on more than a handful of tickets, and stow-related symptoms recur in subsequent, milder wind days.

The 'limit switch bracket bent / reformed / recalibrated' mode recurs on tracker rows already repaired during the burst (repeat asset_id within 6-12 months, recurrence flag true) - one member already carries recurrence=true.
Part consumption is dominated by a narrow set of SKUs (damper, coupling, limit-switch bracket, stow pin) rather than broad structural steel, indicating a repeating weak link.
Sister sites sharing the same tracker OEM/vintage show elevated tracker_structure ticket rates per installed row even in months with no logged wind event.
Post-burst preventive-maintenance or retrofit work orders (stow-logic change, damper upgrade) appear in the record within 6 months.
discriminating_evidence: Normalised ticket rate per installed tracker row at this site versus other sites of the same OEM/vintage in wind-free months: elevated => H2; equal => H1 or H3.
Repeat-visit rate on the same asset_id after the burst closes - high repeat rate is the strongest separator from a one-off event.
Whether recorded/estimated wind speed on 3/14 exceeded the tracker's rated stow wind speed; damage below rating supports H2.
